editorial.headline: Forestry Timber Use: Open Nationally, Conditional in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans the forest-to-log chain, from planting through felling, with full foreign ownership nationally and a 95% ceiling in Bali tied to local-community partnership.
editorial.body:
Pemanfaatan Kayu Hutan is the operational work of managing timber within forest areas, beginning with planting and continuing through to felling, with roundwood as the resulting product. Its scope reaches natural forests, semi-natural forests and planted forests, and specifically includes the use of timber forest products from plantation forests and natural forests in production forests. This is not simply a trading description: it identifies the activity at the point where forest management produces timber.

The code is open across every listed business scale: micro, small, medium and large. Nationally, it is also open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. That national position matters because it makes the ownership ceiling unusually direct: a foreign investor may hold the full business nationally, provided the registered activity is genuinely the forest-management and timber-production work described here.

Bali requires a more careful reading. The provincial status is restricted, not closed, and the record sets a separate Bali ceiling of 95% foreign ownership. That level is available only with a partnership with the local community. The distinction is substantive: the national 100% ceiling does not erase Bali’s stated local condition or its lower provincial cap. A prospective PMA registration in Bali should therefore be framed around a 95% maximum foreign stake and the required local-community partnership, rather than relying on the national position alone.

The provincial setting also includes a permanent, island-wide PMA block for activities classified as Low or Medium-Low risk. The record does not identify this activity’s risk classification, so that wider rule should not be stretched into a claim that this code is blocked. What the record does establish is narrower and clearer: this activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali on a restricted basis, subject to the 95% ceiling and local-community partnership. For founders, the governing question is not whether the activity is nationally open—it is—but whether the Bali structure is built to meet the provincial condition that accompanies it.
